lead: A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when nothing inside it, or between it and its surroundings, is pushing for change: no unbalanced force, no temperature difference, no unfinished reaction. Only then does it have one pressure and one temperature, so only then can its state be drawn as a point. A quasi-static process keeps the system infinitely close to equilibrium all the time by changing it in tiny steps, so the process becomes a continuous line of state points on a p–V diagram and its work can be found as an area. Engine and compressor calculations begin with this idealisation and then correct for the real, faster process.
prereq: You need: state, path and state diagrams.

blocks.text: Thermodynamic equilibrium needs three kinds of balance at once.

items: Thermal equilibrium: one temperature throughout, equal to that of any surroundings it can exchange heat with. Otherwise heat flows and the state drifts.
Mechanical equilibrium: no unbalanced force. The pressure is uniform (apart from small hydrostatic differences) and any piston is at rest.
Chemical equilibrium: no reaction, mixing or diffusion still changing the composition. Some syllabi add phase equilibrium here: no net evaporation or melting.

blocks.text: For gas under a piston at rest, the forces on the piston balance. Upward is the gas pressure on the piston face; downward are the atmosphere, the weight of the piston and any load on it:
p A = pₐₜₘ A + (m + mₛ) g
blocks.where: p is the absolute gas pressure in Pa; A is the piston area in m²; pₐₜₘ is the atmospheric pressure in Pa; m is the piston mass and mₛ the load (sand) on it, in kg; g = 9.81 m/s². Leaving out pₐₜₘ is the most common mistake in these problems.

blocks.text: A practical test of equilibrium is to read the gauges, wait and read again: an isolated system whose readings do not change is in equilibrium. Constant readings alone are not enough when mass or energy is flowing, as the next section shows.

A steam turbine running at full load has steady readings: steam enters at, say, 500 °C and leaves at 60 °C, and each gauge holds still for hours. It is in steady state, not in equilibrium, because steam flows through it and a 440 °C temperature difference drives heat along its casing. Equilibrium has no flows and no gradients; steady state has flows and gradients that do not change with time. A useful exam check: if mass or energy is crossing the boundary, the system is not in equilibrium, however steady the readings.

Dump a heavy weight on a piston and the gas under it is squeezed fast: for a moment the gas next to the piston is at a higher pressure than the gas at the bottom, the piston overshoots and bounces, and eddies swirl. These in-between conditions are not equilibrium states. The gas has no single pressure, so they cannot be plotted as points and the process cannot be drawn as a line; only its start and end states, after everything settles, are known.

Now add the same load one grain of sand at a time, waiting after each grain. Each grain disturbs the gas by an infinitesimal amount, and the gas settles into a new equilibrium state before the next grain. The process passes through a continuous chain of equilibrium states. In the limit of infinitely small steps this is a quasi-static (quasi-equilibrium) process.

items: Make the driving force infinitesimal: one more grain of sand to compress, or one grain removed (or the outside pressure lowered by a tiny dp) to expand.
Wait until the system settles into a new equilibrium state.
Repeat until the final state is reached; each settled state is one point on the p–V diagram.

blocks.text: Because every intermediate state has one p and one V, the process is a line, and the work done at the moving boundary is W = ∫p dV, the area under that line (see displacement work). Infinitely many steps would take infinite time, so a real process is only nearly quasi-static. It is a good approximation when the process is slow compared with the time the gas needs to settle. Pressure evens out at about the speed of sound, roughly 340 m/s in room air, so across a 0.1 m cylinder it takes about 0.3 ms; an engine stroke at 3000 rpm lasts 10 ms, which is why even engine strokes are first analysed as quasi-static.

sections.h3: Quasi-static is not the same as reversible

blocks.text: A process is reversible if system and surroundings can both be returned to their first states with no trace left anywhere. Every reversible process must be quasi-static, but a quasi-static process can still be irreversible. Push a piston in slowly against friction: the gas passes through equilibrium states, yet the friction turns work into heat that will not come back. Stir a gas slowly with a paddle while a piston moves: same result. Reversibility also needs no friction, no heat flow across a finite temperature difference, no unrestrained expansion and no mixing; the full treatment is in reversible and irreversible processes, with the second law.

figure.caption: Left: the piston is at rest when the gas force pA balances the atmosphere, the piston and the sand. Right: the worked example’s states. Adding sand 5 kg at a time gives equilibrium points on the curve pV = constant; dumping all 25 kg at once links the same end states 1 and 2 by states that have no single pressure, so no line can be drawn.

spec.aria: Left: a cylinder with a piston carrying sand; arrows show the gas pressure pushing up and the atmosphere, piston and sand weight pushing down. Right: a p–V plot with six dots from 163.78 kPa at 1.000 litre to 195.00 kPa at 0.840 litre lying on a smooth curve, and a dotted wiggle for the sudden process.

examples.question: A vertical cylinder of diameter 100 mm holds 1.000 litre of air under a frictionless piston of mass 50 kg; the atmosphere is at 101.325 kPa and g = 9.81 m/s². (a) Find the gas pressure when the piston is at rest. (b) Sand is added 5 kg at a time, up to 25 kg, so slowly that the air stays at room temperature (pV constant). Find p and V after each addition. (c) What is the final state, and how would it differ if all 25 kg were dumped at once?
steps: (a) Piston area A = π D²/4 = π × 0.100² ÷ 4 = 7.854 × 10⁻³ m².
Force balance pA = pₐₜₘA + mg gives p = pₐₜₘ + mg/A = 101 325 + (50 × 9.81) ÷ 7.854 × 10⁻³ = 101 325 + 62 452 = 163 777 Pa = 163.78 kPa.
(b) With sand mₛ on the piston: p = 101.325 + (50 + mₛ) × 9.81 ÷ (7.854 × 10⁻³ × 1000) kPa, and V = p₁V₁/p with p₁V₁ = 163.78 kPa × 1.000 L = 163.78 kPa·L = 163.78 J.

Each row is a state in equilibrium (piston at rest, air at room temperature), so each is a point on the p–V diagram. With smaller and smaller sand steps the points join into the curve pV = 163.78 J: a quasi-static path.
(c) Final state: p₂ = 195.00 kPa and V₂ = 0.8399 L; the piston has dropped (1.000 − 0.8399) × 10⁻³ m³ ÷ 7.854 × 10⁻³ m² = 0.0204 m = 20.4 mm.

If all 25 kg were dumped at once, the air would end, after the piston stops bouncing and the air cools back to room temperature, in the same state 2, because the same force balance and temperature fix it. But the states in between would have no single pressure: the process links the same two points without a line, and ∫p dV cannot be evaluated along it.
examples.answer: p₁ = 163.78 kPa; adding 25 kg slowly takes the air through the equilibrium states in the table to p₂ = 195.00 kPa, V₂ = 0.8399 L. The sudden process reaches the same end state but is not quasi-static.

traps: Forgetting the atmosphere in the piston balance: p = mg/A alone gives 62.45 kPa instead of 163.78 kPa in the worked example.
Calling a steady device an equilibrium system. Constant readings with flow through the boundary mean steady state, not equilibrium.
Calling every slow process reversible. A slow process with friction or stirring is quasi-static and irreversible.
Drawing a fast process as a solid line on a p–V diagram. Only its end states are equilibrium states; draw a dashed line, and do not take ∫p dV along it.

quiz.q: Name the three conditions for thermodynamic equilibrium.
quiz.a: Thermal (one temperature, no heat flow), mechanical (no unbalanced force, uniform pressure) and chemical (no reaction or diffusion changing composition).

quiz.q: Why can a quasi-static process be drawn as a line on a p–V diagram while a sudden one cannot?
quiz.a: Each intermediate state of a quasi-static process is an equilibrium state with one p and one V, so it is a point and the points join into a line. In a sudden process the pressure differs from place to place, so there is no point to plot.

quiz.q: Is every quasi-static process reversible? Give a reason.
quiz.a: No. A slow compression against piston friction is quasi-static, but friction turns work into heat that cannot be returned, so it is irreversible.

quiz.q: A 20 kg piston of area 0.010 m² rests on gas; the atmosphere is at 100 kPa and g = 9.81 m/s². Find the gas pressure.
In the worked example, how much sand in total would bring the air to 0.9000 L at room temperature?
The worked example's sudden and slow processes end in the same state. Which quantities are the same for both, and which may differ?
quiz.a: Properties at the end (p₂, V₂, T₂, U₂) are the same because they depend only on the state. Work and heat, being path functions, can differ; the sudden process also cannot be drawn as a line.

beyond: Real compressors and turbines are first sized as quasi-static and reversible, then corrected with an isentropic efficiency measured on test rigs. Finite-time thermodynamics studies engines that must deliver power and so cannot run infinitely slowly. Search next: finite-time thermodynamics, endoreversible engines, relaxation time in gases.
